thread.title: Some companies have to wait for boost from lower tax rates

author: Francine McKenna
title: Some companies have to wait for boost from lower tax rates
text:
Not all companies will report the full positive impact of new lower corporate tax rates right away. 
The Tax Cuts and Job Act, signed into law by President Trump last month, reduced corporate income tax rates from 35% to 21% beginning Jan. 1 and will significantly reduce the amount of taxes paid by all U.S. companies going forward. However, companies that don’t use Dec. 31 as their year end have to wait until fiscal 2019 to enjoy full impact of lower rates.
Companies that do not have a Dec. 31 year-end will have to use a blended old and new rate to calculate their 2018 taxable income.
Take Microsoft MSFT, -0.07% MSFT, -0.07% , for example, which ended its 2017 fiscal year last June 30. Microsoft will have to apply a blended rate of 28%—6 months at 35% and 6 months of 21%—to its fiscal year 2018 taxable income. 
Then the new reduced 21% rate would apply to all future fiscal years.
Other large market cap companies like Microsoft with a non-calendar year-end include Apple AAPL, -0.01% , Sprint S, -1.90% , McKesson MCK, +0.94% , Medtronic MDT, +0.43% and Cardinal Health CAH, +2.88% . 
Accounting standards require deferred tax assets and liabilities to be measured at the new tax rate, but only when temporary differences between financial statement and tax returns such as depreciation and amortization are to be realized or settled. 
See also: New tax law spells big changes for companies’ approach to executive compensation 
Read: These companies will take a huge profit hit from lower tax rates 
That’s why investors are already seeing announcements from several companies forced to take a hit on the re-measurement of deferred tax assets based upon the new 21% tax rate. Under generally accepted accounting principles, the standards almost all U.S.-listed companies follow when reporting their results to the Securities and Exchange Commission, tax assets and liabilities will have to be re-measured during quarter in which the new tax legislation was enacted. In this case that’s the fourth quarter for traditional calendar year-end companies but not for those who don’t use Dec. 31 as their year-end. 
The SEC recently issued guidelines for 8-K filing requirements related to the new tax law. Companies will be required to disclose the estimated impact of the new tax law now through an 8-K filing if it is expected to be material. 
Non-calendar year-end companies will be required to analyze which components of their deferred tax assets will reverse at which rate. The applicable rate is also determined, according to an up-to-the-minute guide published by global accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, by reference to the rate expected to apply when the reversal affects the amount of taxes payable or refundable. 
For example, a June 30 fiscal year company such as Sears Holdings SHLD, -8.48% or a March 30 company like Symantec SYMC, -1.89% that reported losses in 2017 and are expected to generate tax losses in 2018, no taxes would be due and the reversal of the deductible temporary difference would have no impact on taxes payable. As a result, Sears Holdings will measure everything at 21%, which is the rate expected to be in effect in the future when the credit will potentially be needed to offset taxes payable or refundable on net income. 
However, if the company expected to be profitable in 2018, the measurement would be applied at applicable blended tax rate.
